title: Hit Finding: Screening Strategies
summary: How the first active molecules are found.

lessons.title: High-throughput screening

levels.kid: When scientists want a new medicine, they first need a molecule that does at least a little bit of the right thing. So they use robots! The robots drop hundreds of thousands of different molecules into tiny wells on plastic plates, each with the target, like a germ protein. A machine then checks which wells light up or change color, meaning something happened. This is **high-throughput screening**. It is like testing a giant ring of keys on one lock really fast. Only a few keys turn the lock a little, and those become the starting points.
levels.hs:
**High-throughput screening (HTS)** tests huge numbers of compounds, often hundreds of thousands to a few million, against a biological target to find **hits**: molecules that show the desired activity.

How it works:
- Compounds are stored dissolved in DMSO in **compound libraries**.
- Robots dispense tiny volumes into plates with **384 or 1536 wells**.
- Each well contains the assay, such as an enzyme plus a substrate that glows when it reacts.
- Readers measure fluorescence, luminescence or absorbance automatically.

Two main assay types:
- **Biochemical assays** use purified proteins (for example, does the compound stop an enzyme?).
- **Cell-based assays** use living cells (for example, does the compound turn on a reporter gene or change calcium levels?).

Screens usually test each compound once at a single concentration. Typically only a small fraction, often well under 1%, count as hits. Those are then retested to confirm activity and tested at several concentrations to measure potency (IC50).

To trust a screen, scientists check its quality with a statistic called **Z'** (Z-prime), which compares the signal difference between positive and negative controls to their variability. A Z' of 0.5 or higher means an excellent assay.

HTS made drug discovery more industrial, but many hits are false positives, so careful follow-up is essential.
levels.college:
HTS combines assay biology, automation, compound management and informatics.

**Assay formats.** Biochemical readouts include fluorescence intensity, fluorescence polarization (binding of a labeled ligand), FRET and time-resolved FRET (TR-FRET, using lanthanide donors to reduce background), AlphaScreen/AlphaLISA (singlet oxygen transfer between beads) and luminescence (luciferase-coupled ATP detection for kinases). Cell-based formats include reporter genes, calcium-flux assays for GPCRs and ion channels, and **high-content imaging**, which extracts many features per cell.

**Assay quality.** Z' = 1 - 3(SDpos + SDneg)/|mean pos - mean neg|. Values 0.5-1 indicate a robust separation band. Signal-to-background, edge effects, DMSO tolerance and reagent stability are optimized in a pilot screen before full deployment.

**Execution.** Acoustic droplet ejection transfers nanoliter volumes of compound without tips. Primary screens commonly use one concentration in the low micromolar range; hits are defined by a threshold (for example, 3 standard deviations from the neutral control or percent inhibition). **Quantitative HTS (qHTS)** instead tests every compound at several concentrations, producing concentration-response curves from the start.

**Follow-up cascade.** Cherry-picked hits are retested in duplicate, then in concentration-response, then in counterscreens and orthogonal assays. Fresh powder and LC-MS confirm identity and purity, since DMSO stocks degrade and absorb water.

**Library design.** Modern libraries emphasize lead-likeness (lower molecular weight and logP than drugs), removal of reactive and interference-prone compounds, and coverage of diverse scaffolds. Focused libraries target families such as kinases.

**Target-based vs phenotypic.** Target-based HTS identifies modulators of a defined protein; phenotypic screening measures a cellular outcome and later requires target deconvolution.
levels.phd:
The statistical and conceptual foundations of HTS deserve as much attention as automation. A single-point primary screen is a noisy classifier: with hit thresholds set on plate-wise distributions, false positives arise from assay artifacts, random error and systematic plate effects, while false negatives arise from insolubility, compound degradation and threshold choice. Robust normalization (B-score or median polish to correct row and column effects), replicate designs and plate-uniformity studies mitigate systematic error. Because hit rates are low, even a small false-positive rate can produce a hit list dominated by artifacts, a base-rate problem familiar from diagnostic testing.

The chemical-space problem is equally fundamental. Even a few million compounds sample a vanishingly small fraction of drug-like space, estimated at around 10^60 molecules, so HTS success depends on library composition. Historical corporate libraries were biased by past projects, and combinatorial libraries of the 1990s were often flat, lipophilic and poorly diverse, contributing to disappointing returns. Lessons from this era led to emphasis on sp3-rich and natural-product-like collections, fragment libraries, and later DNA-encoded and virtual make-on-demand libraries that reach billions of molecules.

Assay biology determines what hits mean. Biochemical assays run at substrate concentrations near Km detect competitive, uncompetitive and noncompetitive inhibitors with different sensitivities; running ATP-competitive kinase screens at physiological ATP shifts hits toward tighter binders. Cellular screens capture permeability and pathway context but introduce cytotoxicity, off-target and transcriptional artifacts. Phenotypic screens have historically delivered a disproportionate number of first-in-class drugs, according to an influential analysis of approvals from 1999 to 2008, but with the cost of target deconvolution.

Finally, HTS data are a resource: public repositories such as PubChem BioAssay and ChEMBL enable frequent-hitter analyses, machine learning models of activity and interference, and retrospective analysis of which chemotypes are promiscuous across many assays.
levels.expert:
A senior screening scientist thinks about HTS as a decision pipeline whose output must be a few validated chemical series, not a long list of hits.

Before screening, they ask whether the assay answers the right biological question. Is the protein construct physiologically relevant (full-length vs catalytic domain, correct post-translational modifications)? Is the substrate concentration chosen to find the desired mechanism? Is there a tool compound to serve as a positive control? Pilot screens of a few thousand compounds, including known actives, reveal plate effects and estimate hit rates before committing a million-compound campaign.

During triage, experienced teams expect artifacts. They plan counterscreens from the outset, such as running a luciferase-only assay for luciferase-coupled readouts, adding detergent to detect aggregators, or using a different detection technology. They flag frequent hitters from historical data. They reorder or resynthesize compounds, because the identity of a decades-old DMSO stock is uncertain.

Resource reality also matters. A full HTS campaign is expensive in protein, reagents and robotics time, so many organizations now combine approaches: a smaller diverse HTS set, a fragment screen, a DNA-encoded library selection and a virtual screen run in parallel, choosing whichever yields the best chemical starting points. Academic centers and consortia make HTS available to university labs and rare-disease foundations.

Translational examples show its value. Ivacaftor, a CFTR potentiator for cystic fibrosis, came from a cell-based HTS that read out CFTR channel function, followed by medicinal chemistry, and transformed care for patients with specific CFTR mutations. Many kinase inhibitors trace back to biochemical HTS hits. In neuroscience, cell-based screens on patient-derived neurons and organoids are increasingly used to find compounds that rescue disease-relevant phenotypes, though reproducibility and scale remain challenging.

The practical rule: a hit is a hypothesis, and the screening team's job is to falsify bad ones quickly.

keyPoints: HTS tests hundreds of thousands to millions of compounds in 384- or 1536-well plates.
Biochemical assays use purified proteins; cell-based assays use living cells.
Z' of 0.5 or higher marks a robust assay.
Hit rates are low, often below 1%, and include many false positives.
Hits are confirmed by retesting, dose-response, counterscreens and fresh samples.

Most false positives share a common impurity across unrelated library members
Assay noise increases chiefly when the compound concentration is lowered
advancedTest.explain: Rare true positives are outnumbered by false ones.

advancedTest.explain: A CFTR potentiator for cystic fibrosis.

lessons.title: DNA-encoded libraries

levels.kid: Imagine you have a billion tiny toy pieces, and each one wears a little name tag made of DNA, the same stuff in your genes. You pour them all into one cup with a protein you want to grab. The pieces that stick hold on, and the rest are washed away. Then scientists read the DNA name tags of the sticky ones, like scanning barcodes at a store. Now they know which molecules grabbed the protein! This trick is called a **DNA-encoded library**, and it lets scientists test billions of molecules in one small tube.
levels.hs:
A **DNA-encoded library (DEL)** is a huge collection of small molecules, each attached to a short DNA strand that acts as a **barcode** recording how it was made.

How libraries are made (split and pool):
1. Start with a DNA "headpiece" attached to a chemical handle.
2. Split it into many portions. Add a different building block to each portion, plus a matching DNA tag.
3. Pool everything, then split again and add a second building block with a second tag.
4. Repeat a few cycles.

With 1,000 building blocks in each of three cycles, you get 1,000 x 1,000 x 1,000 = **a billion** different molecules, all in one tube.

How they are screened:
- The target protein is attached to beads.
- The whole library is mixed with it. Molecules that bind stay; the rest are washed away.
- The bound molecules' DNA barcodes are copied by **PCR** and read by **DNA sequencing**.
- Barcodes that appear far more often than expected point to binders.

Advantages: billions of compounds, small amounts of protein, low cost per compound.

Limitations: the chemistry must not damage DNA, the DNA tag may affect binding, and binding does not prove the molecule works. Hits must be **made again without DNA** and tested in normal assays.
levels.college:
DEL technology, proposed by Brenner and Lerner in 1992, became practical with next-generation sequencing. Libraries are most often built by **split-and-pool** synthesis with enzymatic ligation of double-stranded DNA codons after each chemistry step; alternatives include DNA-templated synthesis, in which hybridization brings reactants together.

**DNA-compatible chemistry.** Reactions must run in water or mixed aqueous-organic solvent, at low concentration, near-neutral pH, without strongly acidic conditions that cause depurination, and without metals or oxidants that damage DNA. Workhorse reactions include amide coupling, reductive amination, SNAr, Suzuki-Miyaura coupling under DNA-compatible conditions, sulfonylation, urea formation and copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition. Expanding this toolbox is an active field (photoredox, on-DNA C-H functionalization).

**Selection.** Libraries are incubated with immobilized, tagged protein (His-tag or biotin), washed, and eluted, often by heat. Controls include beads without protein and protein with a known competitive ligand, which distinguishes active-site binders from binders elsewhere. Sequencing counts are converted into **enrichment** statistics; clusters of related enriched molecules (for example, sharing two of three building blocks) form **SAR lines** that are more trustworthy than single sequences.

**Off-DNA resynthesis.** Enriched structures are made without DNA, often with a small group mimicking the linker attachment point, and tested for affinity and function.

**Limitations.** Truncated or failed products carry valid barcodes; reaction yields vary across building blocks; three-cycle libraries skew toward high molecular weight; and binders may be driven partly by the DNA-linker interface.

**Successes.** DEL produced clinical candidates such as GSK's RIPK1 inhibitor GSK2982772 and soluble epoxide hydrolase inhibitors, and is widely used for difficult targets.
levels.phd:
DEL selection is best understood as an affinity-enrichment experiment with Poisson sampling noise. Each library member is present at very low copy number (often thousands to a few million copies across the selection), so sequencing counts for any individual compound are small and statistically fragile. Analysis therefore relies on normalized enrichment ratios with confidence intervals, comparison against no-target and competitor controls, and aggregation by building-block combinations (disynthons) to recover signals hidden in noise. Enrichment correlates only loosely with affinity, as it also reflects synthesis yield, linker effects and off-rate during washing.

Library design follows several principles: maximizing chemical diversity and drug-likeness per cycle, using two-cycle libraries for lower molecular weight, incorporating sp3-rich and macrocyclic scaffolds, and covalent libraries carrying electrophiles to find covalent ligands. Fidelity matters: quality-control experiments measure conversion for each building block, and building blocks below a yield threshold are excluded.

DEL also enables selections impossible with plate-based HTS: against protein complexes, in the presence of competitor ligands to find allosteric binders, under different protein conformations, or in cells and cell lysates. Selections against E3 ligases have identified new ligands for targeted protein degradation, and ternary selections can search for molecular glue-like behavior.

The largest recent development is integration with machine learning. Because DEL generates millions of positive and negative data points per target, models trained on enrichment data can generalize to commercially available or make-on-demand compounds not in the library, then predict binders that are purchased and tested off-DNA. This decouples the DEL experiment from its own chemistry and has yielded hits with novel scaffolds. Benchmarks and open data sets (for example, public DEL selection data) are emerging to evaluate these models.

Key unresolved issues include accurate affinity ranking from counts, the influence of DNA on binding conformations, and broader DNA-compatible reactivity, especially reactions forming sp3-rich bonds.
levels.expert:
In practice, a DEL campaign is attractive when protein is available in small amounts, when HTS is too expensive or impossible, or when a team wants many diverse starting points quickly. Senior scientists approach it with clear rules.

First, protein quality determines everything. The target must be pure, correctly folded and stable on beads, and tag placement must not block the binding site. Selections are usually run with several conditions: target alone, target plus a known inhibitor (to classify binding site), and blank beads. Signals that disappear in the competitor condition are likely active-site binders; signals that remain may be allosteric or nonspecific.

Second, trust patterns, not singletons. Experienced teams look for enrichment shared by families of related compounds, and they discount sequences enriched in blank selections, which often include sticky, polyaromatic or highly charged molecules.

Third, plan resynthesis carefully. Off-DNA compounds are typically made with a capped linker stub, and some lose activity when the DNA is removed because the conjugate contributed to binding. Confirmation uses biophysical methods such as surface plasmon resonance and functional assays.

Fourth, expect property challenges. Three-cycle hits are often large and lipophilic, so the medicinal chemist's next job is to trim nonessential building blocks and raise ligand efficiency, sometimes using structure from crystallography.

DEL has broadened access to targets once considered hard, including protein-protein interactions and E3 ligases, and partnerships with specialized providers mean even small biotech companies can screen billions of compounds. For neuroscience, DEL hits against brain targets still must pass the stricter property filters needed to cross the blood-brain barrier, which the first DEL hit rarely satisfies. The best programs treat DEL as one input among several hit-finding methods and integrate its data with structure-based design and machine learning.

keyPoints: DELs attach a DNA barcode to every small molecule, recording its synthesis.
Split-and-pool synthesis with three cycles of 1,000 building blocks yields a billion compounds.
Affinity selection on immobilized protein, then PCR and sequencing, identifies enriched binders.
Chemistry must be DNA-compatible (aqueous, mild, no strong acid).
Hits must be resynthesized off-DNA and confirmed; binding does not prove function.

examples.tr: Divide, add building block plus DNA codon, pool, repeat.
Sequence counts above expectation indicate binders.
RIPK1 inhibitor clinical candidate originating from DEL screening.

choices: Counts measure binding free energy without dependence on synthesis yield
Enrichment depends on DNA sequence alone and not on selection conditions
A low-count sequence is a proven high-affinity binder
Counts also reflect synthesis yield, linker effects and Poisson noise
advancedTest.explain: Low copy numbers make counts noisy.

advancedTest.q: How has machine learning extended DEL beyond its own library?
choices: Models learn DNA sequence and directly predict cellular metabolism
Models trained on enrichment data predict binders among purchasable compounds
Models replace off-DNA experiments with precise binding constants
Models predict chemical supply shortages rather than target binding
advancedTest.explain: Predicted compounds are tested off-DNA.

advancedTest.explain: Bead enrichment signals stickiness, not target binding.

advancedTest.q: Disynthon analysis means:
choices: Aggregating counts across compounds sharing two building blocks
Comparing two unrelated library members with identical DNA barcodes
Counting compounds built from a single monomer
Discarding pairwise building-block patterns to analyze singletons
advancedTest.explain: It boosts statistical power.

lessons.title: Virtual screening

levels.kid: Testing real molecules in a lab costs time and money. So scientists also test them inside a computer first! If they know the 3D shape of a protein's pocket, the computer tries fitting millions or even billions of pretend molecules into it, like trying puzzle pieces in a hole. Each fit gets a score. The best-scoring ones are then bought or made and tested for real. This is **virtual screening**. The computer is not perfect, and it often guesses wrong, but it helps scientists pick which few molecules are worth trying.
levels.hs:
**Virtual screening** uses computers to search large collections of molecules for likely hits before any lab testing. Only the top-ranked compounds are bought or made and tested.

Two main approaches:

**1. Structure-based (docking).** If the 3D structure of the target protein is known (from X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM or a reliable model), a docking program places each molecule into the binding pocket in many positions (**poses**) and estimates how well it fits using a **scoring function**. Examples of docking programs include AutoDock Vina, Glide and DOCK.

**2. Ligand-based.** If you know some active molecules but not the protein structure, you search for molecules that are similar to them. Methods include:
- **2D similarity** using molecular fingerprints compared by the Tanimoto score
- **Pharmacophore** searches, matching the 3D arrangement of key features like hydrogen-bond donors and aromatic rings
- **Shape similarity**
- **Machine learning** models trained on known actives and inactives

Why use it?
- It can search billions of "make-on-demand" compounds that do not physically exist yet but can be made quickly.
- It is cheap and fast compared with testing every compound.

Limitations: scoring functions are rough, proteins move, and water molecules and charges are hard to model. Many top-scoring molecules do nothing in the lab, so experimental testing is always required.
levels.college:
**Docking** has two parts: a search algorithm that samples ligand conformations, orientations and positions in the binding site, and a scoring function that ranks them. Scoring functions may be physics-based (force-field terms for van der Waals and electrostatics with desolvation corrections), empirical (weighted terms fitted to affinity data), knowledge-based (statistical potentials from crystal structures) or machine-learned. They predict binding poses reasonably well for many targets but rank affinities poorly.

**Preparation matters.** Proteins need correct protonation states (histidines, aspartates), relevant tautomers, retained structural waters and, often, several conformations (ensemble docking) to account for flexibility. Ligand libraries need enumerated protonation states, tautomers and stereoisomers.

**Ligand-based methods.** Extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFP4) encode circular substructures; Tanimoto similarity above roughly 0.4-0.5 suggests related activity, though activity cliffs break this assumption. Pharmacophore models abstract features (donor, acceptor, aromatic, hydrophobic, charged) and their distances. QSAR and machine-learning models predict activity from descriptors.

**Validation.** Retrospective enrichment tests whether known actives rank above decoys (property-matched inactives, as in the DUD-E benchmark), using metrics like enrichment factor and ROC AUC. However, retrospective success can be inflated by decoy bias, so prospective testing is the true measure.

**Ultra-large libraries.** Make-on-demand collections such as Enamine REAL contain billions of compounds synthesizable in weeks with high success. A landmark 2019 study docked about 170 million molecules against the AmpC beta-lactamase and the D4 dopamine receptor, finding potent novel ligands and showing that hit rates and potency improved as library size grew.

**Hit rates.** Prospective virtual screens often report higher hit rates than random HTS, since compounds are preselected for complementarity.
levels.phd:
The central problem of structure-based virtual screening is that scoring functions approximate binding free energy crudely: they neglect or simplify conformational entropy, desolvation, polarization, protein reorganization and the thermodynamics of displaced water. Consequently, docking is better at enrichment, separating likely binders from obvious non-binders, than at ranking affinity. As library size grows into the billions, the number of false positives that score well by chance also grows, because rare artifacts that exploit scoring-function weaknesses become numerous. Ultra-large docking studies report that improved potency with library size coexists with this risk, and that visual inspection by experienced chemists, filters for strain and unsatisfied polar groups, and clustering remain important.

Computational scaling is addressed by hierarchical approaches: synthon-based methods (such as V-SYNTHES) dock fragments representing reagents, then expand only promising combinations; active learning trains a surrogate model on a fraction of docking scores to predict which molecules to dock next, recovering most top-scoring compounds at a small fraction of the cost.

Rigorous physics-based methods, such as free-energy perturbation (FEP) and absolute binding free energy calculations, can rank compounds far better than docking but cost much more; they are typically applied to rescoring or lead optimization. Coupling docking for broad search with free-energy methods for refinement is a common pipeline.

Predicted protein structures have changed the landscape. AlphaFold models allow docking to targets without experimental structures, and prospective campaigns have found ligands against such models, sometimes at hit rates similar to those against crystal structures, although side-chain accuracy, apo-state pocket geometry and missing ligands complicate results. Co-folding methods that predict protein-ligand complexes directly are being evaluated, with concerns about memorization of training data and physically implausible poses.

Finally, generative models invert the problem, designing molecules for a pocket rather than searching libraries; their outputs must be filtered for synthesizability and validated experimentally, as with any virtual screening hypothesis.
levels.expert:
A senior computational chemist treats virtual screening as an experiment with explicit controls and a budget, not a black box.

Before a campaign, they validate the setup. Can docking reproduce known ligand poses (redocking and cross-docking)? Does it enrich known actives over property-matched decoys? Which waters or metal ions must be kept? For flexible targets, they choose multiple receptor conformations, often from crystal structures with different ligands or molecular dynamics snapshots.

During selection, they never simply buy the top 100 scores. They cluster the top ranks, remove compounds with strained conformations or buried polar groups lacking hydrogen bonds, check for reactivity or assay-interference motifs, and pick diverse chemotypes. Experienced modelers inspect poses visually, because the human eye catches unrealistic interactions that scoring misses.

After testing, they measure the true hit rate and potencies, feed results back into models, and quickly test analogs from the same make-on-demand space ("SAR by catalog") to confirm genuine structure-activity relationships. A cluster of related actives is far more convincing than a single potent singleton.

For central nervous system targets, filters for blood-brain barrier penetration (lower polar surface area, fewer hydrogen-bond donors, moderate lipophilicity and avoidance of efflux-prone features) are often applied early, using scores such as CNS MPO, because a beautiful binder that cannot reach the brain is not useful.

Common pitfalls include docking into an apo structure whose pocket is collapsed, ignoring the protonation state of a catalytic residue, trusting retrospective enrichment built on biased decoys, and confusing high docking scores with potency. The best groups pair computation with fast experimental feedback, using biophysical assays and crystallography to verify binding modes. The trend is toward hybrid campaigns that run virtual, DEL and fragment screens in parallel and let the data decide.

keyPoints: Virtual screening ranks compounds computationally before lab testing.
Structure-based docking samples poses in a pocket and scores them; ligand-based methods use similarity, pharmacophores and ML.
Scoring functions predict poses better than affinities; all hits need experimental testing.
Make-on-demand libraries let docking explore billions of synthesizable compounds.
Validation uses enrichment of known actives over decoys, but prospective testing is the true test.

lessons.title: PAINS & assay artifacts

levels.kid: A science test can be tricked. Imagine a test where a good molecule makes a light turn off. Some molecules turn off the light without doing the good thing at all! They might cover the light, clump together like soap bubbles, or break the test machine. Scientists call these **false positives**. Some molecules have shapes that often trick tests, and chemists call them PAINS. A warning label does not mean the molecule is always bad. The smart move is to try a different kind of test and see whether it still works.
levels.hs:
In drug screening, a **false positive** is a compound that looks active in the assay but does not really affect the intended target. **PAINS** stands for pan-assay interference compounds: structural motifs flagged because they appeared as frequent hitters in several assays.

How compounds can fool us:
- **Colloidal aggregation:** molecules form tiny clumps that trap and disable many proteins nonspecifically. A little nonionic detergent often breaks the clumps.
- **Fluorescence interference:** a colored or glowing molecule changes the assay signal without touching the protein.
- **Redox cycling:** some compounds produce reactive oxygen species in the test tube that damage proteins.
- **Chemical reactivity:** a reactive molecule sticks to many proteins, not just the target.
- **Reporter inhibition:** a molecule blocks the light-producing enzyme luciferase, which can make a reporter assay seem positive.

PAINS motifs include rhodanines, catechols and quinones, but **the filter is only a warning, not a verdict**: some useful drugs contain these groups.

How to check: repeat the test with a different method (**orthogonal assay**), check whether adding detergent removes activity, run a test without the target to catch signal interference, and see whether closely related molecules show sensible changes in potency (**SAR**). A hit that disappears in the second assay was likely a trick.
levels.college:
**PAINS** filters were proposed by Baell and Holloway (2010) after analysis of frequent hitters in AlphaScreen assays, identifying substructures such as rhodanines, quinones, catechols and certain heteroaromatics. They are statistical alerts, not proof of promiscuity: catechols are found in valid drugs, and the original data set was biased toward a particular assay platform. Conversely, compounds without PAINS motifs can be equally troublesome.

**Aggregation** occurs when moderately hydrophobic compounds self-assemble into 50- to 500-nanometer colloids that adsorb and inactivate proteins. It creates steep Hill slopes, time dependence and apparent inhibition of unrelated enzymes. Adding 0.01% nonionic detergent (Triton X-100 or Tween-20), raising protein concentration, dynamic light scattering and centrifugation help diagnose it.

**Optical interference:** colored compounds absorb excitation or emission light; autofluorescent compounds emit independently of the reporter. In FRET, they can quench donor or acceptor. In luciferase assays, direct luciferase inhibition or stabilization can distort readouts. AlphaScreen can be fooled by singlet-oxygen quenchers, metal chelators or compounds that disrupt bead interactions.

**Redox cyclers** such as quinones generate hydrogen peroxide in buffers with reducing agents (DTT), nonspecifically oxidizing cysteines. Catalase rescue and peroxide assays expose the artifact.

**Reactivity:** Michael acceptors, aldehydes and other electrophiles can covalently modify many proteins. A covalent warhead can be a valid drug (as in ibrutinib), but it needs selectivity and mechanistic evidence.

**Cell-based artifacts** include general cytotoxicity, membrane disruption and effects on reporters rather than the intended biology.

The antidote is orthogonal confirmation: a different readout, a different protein construct, direct binding measurements and counterscreens against unrelated targets.
levels.phd:
PAINS illustrates how a useful heuristic became an overused binary rule. The original 480 structural filters were derived from six AlphaScreen campaigns, and subsequent analyses found strong platform dependence: a motif may be enriched as an artifact in one format and yield genuine ligands in another. The key statistical problem is base-rate shift. A filter trained on a collection of frequent hitters should not be applied as a categorical judgment to a different chemical library and assay system without validation. Some famously flagged substructures occur in approved drugs, and promiscuity itself can sometimes be the desired mechanism (for example, redox-active anticancer agents).

**Aggregation** is thermodynamically nuanced. Above a critical aggregation concentration, colloids form and adsorb proteins; the apparent IC50 depends on protein concentration, incubation time and buffer conditions, not intrinsic binding affinity. Typical clues include detergent sensitivity, steep Hill slopes (>1.5), noncompetitive-looking enzyme inhibition and inhibition of a counter-enzyme. Aggregates can also confound cell assays via membrane adsorption. Detergent rescue is strong but not absolute evidence, because detergents can perturb legitimate protein-ligand interactions.

**Assay-specific traps** often escape structural filters. In luciferase reporter assays, inhibitors of luciferase may paradoxically increase light after prolonged incubation by stabilizing the enzyme against degradation, producing apparent pathway activation. In AlphaScreen, colorants, singlet-oxygen scavengers and biotin-like compounds can perturb bead readouts. In zinc-dependent proteases, nonspecific metal chelators look active; adding zinc or running an unrelated metalloenzyme counterscreen helps.

**Covalent promiscuity** is better characterized by chemoproteomics than by an electrophile alert alone. Activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) maps cellular targets of reactive fragments. ALARM NMR detects unwanted reactivity with a reporter protein in the presence of reducing agents. Time-dependent inhibition and washout experiments help separate covalent binding from reversible inhibition.

A rigorous policy is therefore: mark suspect compounds, then measure mechanism, target engagement and SAR. Flat SAR across many modifications is often a stronger warning than any structural alert.
levels.expert:
In a real hit-triage meeting, the team asks not 'Does it match a PAINS filter?' but 'What observation would prove this activity is real?'

For a fluorescent enzyme assay hit, they repeat the measurement with an unrelated readout such as LC-MS product quantification, measure direct fluorescence of the compound, vary substrate concentration and add a counterscreen enzyme. For a suspected aggregator, they repeat with and without detergent and at different protein concentrations, and check by dynamic light scattering. For a redox cycler, they add catalase and run a peroxide assay. For a reactive compound, they use glutathione trapping, time-dependent inhibition and proteomics.

The most persuasive test is an **orthogonal assay**: change the readout without changing the biological question. A hit that inhibits the target in fluorescence, SPR binding and a cellular target-engagement assay, and has consistent SAR, deserves investment even if it has a flagged motif. A hit that acts only in the first reporter system does not.

A cautionary story: hundreds of papers reported curcumin as active against unrelated targets, yet its instability, assay interference and poor bioavailability made many mechanistic claims unreliable. This does not mean turmeric is harmful; it means a hit's popularity is not evidence of specific target engagement.

In neuroscience, autofluorescent compounds can look like they rescue neurons in image-based assays, and general cytotoxicity can masquerade as reduced aggregation of a disease protein simply because fewer cells remain. Counterstaining for cell number and using independent readouts is essential.

Medicinal chemists also distinguish deliberate covalent inhibitors (ibrutinib, osimertinib) from nonspecific electrophiles: the former show saturable, site-directed target engagement, clean proteomic selectivity and rational SAR; the latter bind whatever is available. The goal is to reject false hypotheses early, not to ban whole chemical families.

keyPoints: PAINS are statistical structural alerts, not automatic disqualifiers.
Aggregates inhibit unrelated proteins; detergent and DLS help detect them.
Fluorescence, luciferase, redox cycling and reactive groups can fool assays.
Orthogonal assays and counterscreens distinguish real target activity from artifacts.
Consistent structure-activity relationships support a hit; flat SAR raises suspicion.

lessons.title: Hit triage & validation

levels.kid: A molecule that looked good in the first test is called a **hit**. But one lucky test is not enough. First scientists get a fresh, clean sample and test it again. Then they try a different kind of test. They also try changing the molecule a little: if those changes make it work better or worse in a sensible way, the hit is probably real. Last, they make sure it doesn't hurt healthy cells. Only the best hits become **leads**, the molecules chemists spend time improving into medicine candidates.
levels.hs:
A **hit** is a promising result from a screen, not yet a drug. **Hit triage** means deciding which hits are real and worth improving.

A sensible checklist:
1. **Retest** the original sample and make or buy a fresh one. Verify its identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR.
2. Run a **concentration-response curve**: real hits usually show stronger effects as concentration rises, giving an IC50 or EC50.
3. Use an **orthogonal assay**, with a different readout, to rule out a test trick.
4. Measure **direct binding** to the target with tools such as surface plasmon resonance (SPR), which detects binding in real time.
5. Test other proteins and human cells to see if the hit is selective and not generally toxic.
6. Make or buy **close analogs**. Do small changes have predictable effects? This is **structure-activity relationship (SAR)**.

A good hit has reproducible activity, real target binding, a workable chemical structure, reasonable selectivity, and a way to make analogs. A **lead** is a hit family strong enough to invest in; a **candidate** is the optimized molecule selected for testing in people.

Teams usually keep multiple chemical series at first, because many fail later from poor absorption, safety problems or lack of novelty.
levels.college:
Hit triage separates biological truth from assay artifacts and chemistry risk. A useful cascade moves from high-throughput to low-throughput, orthogonal evidence.

**Identity and purity:** LC-MS checks mass and chromatography, 1H NMR confirms structure and stereochemistry if relevant; fresh synthesis rules out degraded DMSO stocks. Impurities can create false activity.

**Potency and mechanism:** concentration-response curves across a broad range provide IC50 (biochemical) or EC50 (cell-based), with Hill slopes near 1 for simple 1:1 binding. Varying substrate concentration distinguishes competitive from noncompetitive inhibition via enzyme kinetics.

**Direct binding:** SPR measures association/dissociation (kon, koff, KD), isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) gives affinity and enthalpy, differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) measures thermal stabilization, and ligand-observed NMR (STD-NMR, WaterLOGSY) detects weak fragment binding. Each has artifacts (DSF shifts are not proof of binding, SPR can be distorted by aggregation).

**Cellular target engagement:** cellular thermal shift assays (CETSA), NanoBRET tracer displacement and chemical-probe competition test whether the compound reaches and binds its target inside cells.

**SAR:** an analog series should show interpretable potency shifts; flat SAR is a red flag. **Ligand efficiency (LE)** = -DeltaG binding divided by the number of heavy atoms (roughly 1.37 x pKD / heavy atoms, in kcal/mol per heavy atom), favoring small efficient hits; **lipophilic ligand efficiency (LLE)** = pIC50 - logD measures potency not bought solely through grease.

**Developability:** solubility, permeability, metabolic stability, hERG and selectivity panels are screened early. Chemical novelty and patentability also affect value.

A portfolio often keeps two or three unrelated hit series to hedge risk.
levels.phd:
Validation is best framed as converging independent lines of evidence with different failure modes. A biochemical IC50, SPR KD and cellular EC50 need not match exactly: IC50 depends on substrate concentration and mechanism (Cheng-Prusoff for competitive inhibitors), SPR measures binding to purified protein under immobilization, and cell EC50 convolves permeability, efflux, binding to serum proteins, metabolism and target abundance. But if they disagree by several orders of magnitude, the team needs a mechanistic explanation rather than optimism.

**Kinetics** matter beyond equilibrium affinity. Slow dissociation can yield long target residence time, especially valuable when free drug exposure fluctuates. SPR sensorgrams should be checked for mass transport limitation and nonspecific surface binding. ITC can resolve enthalpy-entropy compensation; DSF stabilization can be absent for a genuine ligand that stabilizes an inactive conformation. Orthogonal biophysics catches method-specific artifacts.

**Mechanism of action** is triangulated with resistance mutations, CRISPR knockdown or knockout, target overexpression, chemical-genetic interactions and structural biology. An inhibitor that still acts in a target-knockout cell likely has another target. For phenotypic hits, chemoproteomics with photoaffinity or clickable probes helps identify binding partners.

**Efficiency metrics** require caveats. LE compares small fragments to larger hits but is biased by molecular size; LLE can reward overly polar compounds with no permeability; and pIC50 estimates affinity only under appropriate assay conditions. Multiparameter optimization later must balance potency, properties and liability in the relevant compartment.

**Triage decisions** are Bayesian in spirit: a lone spectacular IC50 from a single-point screen has low prior credibility, while modest reproducible potency backed by orthogonal binding, a crystal structure and clean SAR is more likely to mature. Companies use chemical-series clustering and select a diversified portfolio to avoid correlated failure.

Finally, reproducibility demands rigorous compound registration, counterion and tautomer tracking, assay metadata, controls and versioned data so a team can reconstruct what was actually tested months later.
levels.expert:
The senior medicinal chemist's first question after a hit list is: Which results will survive contact with a real compound and a living cell?

A strong validation package includes fresh resynthesis, identity and purity proof, concentration-response in at least two independent assay technologies, direct binding, biochemical selectivity, cellular target engagement and interpretable analog SAR. Structural proof of a bound pose by X-ray or cryo-EM is powerful but not always needed at the hit stage. The team looks for more than potency: synthetic accessibility, solubility, permeability, chemical stability and freedom from hERG or mitochondrial liabilities.

A special concern for neurological drugs is brain exposure. A hit can inhibit an enzyme beautifully but fail because it is pumped out of the brain by P-glycoprotein or binds plasma proteins too tightly. Teams measure unbound brain-to-plasma partitioning (Kp,uu) and target engagement in the brain, not just total drug levels. This explains why many early neuro hits fail to become treatments.

Chemists also perform an early 'kill experiment': if a molecule is suspected of binding nonspecifically, test against unrelated proteins; if it is claimed to act through a receptor, remove that receptor genetically and check whether the phenotype disappears. Killing a bad series in a week is a success, not a failure.

When choosing a lead, teams compare hit families rather than individual molecules. One series may have fantastic potency but insolubility and difficult chemistry; another has moderate potency, clean selectivity and easy analog synthesis, making it the better lead. In drug discovery, the prettiest number is rarely the best decision.

The final product of triage is a documented hypothesis: this chemical series binds this target in this way, acts in cells for a reason supported by data, and can plausibly be improved. Everything else goes back to the idea pile.

keyPoints: A hit is a hypothesis; confirm with fresh compound, identity and purity checks.
Run concentration-response curves and orthogonal assays with different readouts.
Direct binding tools include SPR, ITC, DSF and NMR; cell engagement tests target access.
Consistent SAR, selectivity and workable chemistry distinguish a lead from a false hit.
Keep multiple unrelated series to diversify risk.
